extracted.intended_audience: journalism researchers, media scholars, journalism students and news professionals
extracted.subtask_description: An updated taxonomy of news values (criteria journalists use to select and present stories), including items that reflect digital/social media dynamics such as shareability and audio-visual appeal. Intended as a descriptive/analytic tool for studying news selection across platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusivity: Stories generated by, or available first to, the news organisation as a result of interviews, letters, investigations, surveys, polls, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include original interviews, investigations, surveys or letters; exclusives can raise a story's newsworthiness by offering unique material not available elsewhere. Availability of resources and time affects the ability to secure exclusives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad news
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad news: Stories with particularly negative overtones such as death, injury, defeat and loss (of a job, for example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad-news framing commonly increases prominence and audience interest; the study finds bad news remains an important factor both in print and online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Conﬂict: Stories concerning conﬂict such as controversies, arguments, splits, strikes, ﬁghts, insurrections and warfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict and controversy are durable news values (supported by prior scholarship); they often interact with exclusivity and follow-up coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprise: Stories that have an element of surprise, contrast and/or the unusual about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unusual or unexpected elements can make otherwise routine events newsworthy; surprise often overlaps with drama and entertainment values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio-visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Audio-visuals: Stories that have arresting photographs, video, audio and/or which can be illustrated with infographics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors emphasise the growing importance of arresting audio-visuals—photos, video, infographics—for selection and shareability online; visuals can enable data or slowly unfolding events to become popular (e.g. infographics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareability
rubrics_metrics.description: Shareability: Stories that are thought likely to generate sharing and comments via Facebook, Twitter and other forms of social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shareability is hard to define precisely but appears increasingly important. Gibson's characterization—'stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you angry'—is cited. Visual-led items often score highly for shareability; social-platform differences (Facebook vs Twitter) shape which stories spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment: Soft stories concerning sex, showbusiness, sport, lighter human interest, animals, or offering opportunities for humorous treatment, witty headlines or lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entertainment (soft news) is prominent among most-shared social media items; such items may be selected because they are enjoyable and easily shared, especially on Facebook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama: Stories concerning an unfolding drama such as escapes, accidents, searches, sieges, rescues, battles or court cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing, unfolding events with drama attract attention and often generate follow-up coverage; drama intersects with surprise and magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow-up: Stories about subjects already in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that continue or update earlier coverage tend to be prioritized; follow-up value helps sustain audience interest over time and supports serial reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: The power elite
rubrics_metrics.description: The power elite: Stories concerning powerful individuals, organisations, institutions or corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items involving powerful actors are classic news values; however, the study finds power-elite stories are less prominent in the most-shared social-media lists compared with other values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevance: Stories about groups or nations perceived to be inﬂuential with, or culturally or historically familiar to, the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance depends on the target audience's cultural, historical or political affinities; perceived closeness increases newsworthiness for a particular readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnitude: Stories perceived as sufﬁciently signiﬁcant in the large numbers of people involved or in potential impact, or involving a degree of extreme behaviour or extreme occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale impact, high numbers affected, or extremity of behaviour increase prominence; magnitude often combines with bad/good news and drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Celebrity: Stories concerning people who are already famous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Celebrity stories attract attention and can drive sharing, though the paper notes celebrity did not dominate social-media shares in their 2014 sample as might be expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good news
rubrics_metrics.description: Good news: Stories with particularly positive overtones such as recoveries, break-throughs, cures, wins and celebrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive-framed stories can be newsworthy and shareable (e.g. uplifting human-interest pieces); good-news stories contrast with bad-news but both influence selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: News organisation’s agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: News organisation’s agenda: Stories that set or ﬁt the news organisation’s own agenda, whether ideological, commercial or as part of a speciﬁc campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial or commercial agendas shape selection and treatment; agenda-setting can override other news values when organisations push ideological or campaign priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints and subjective influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical and subjective influences: News-value application is governed by practical considerations (availability of resources and time) and subjective, often unconscious influences (social, educational, ideological and cultural influences on journalists, workplace position, type of audience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors emphasise that selection depends not only on inherent news values but also on who is selecting, for whom, in what medium, and with what resources; online pressures for clicks and shares will influence selection and treatment. This taxonomy is presented as a tool for analysis and discussion, not as a definitive or universally prescriptive list.
